result.summary: Thracian women, maddened by Bacchic rites, murder Orpheus on Mount Rhodope after his music fails to stop their weapons. His head and lyre float down the Hebrus to Lesbos, where a serpent is turned to stone, and his ghost rejoins Eurydice below. Bacchus then punishes the women by turning them into trees.

scenes.title: Argument of the fable
scenes.summary: A prose summary states that the women kill Orpheus, his head reaches Lesbos, a serpent becomes stone and the killers become trees.

scenes.title: The murder of Orpheus
scenes.summary: The Ciconian women attack Orpheus; spears and stones are at first charmed, but the din drowns his music and they tear him apart with farm tools. All nature mourns him.
scenes.stakes: Orpheus's life is at stake as the frenzied women overpower his music.

scenes.title: Head and lyre reach Lesbos
scenes.summary: His limbs are scattered; the head and lyre float down the Hebrus, still sounding, to Lesbos, where Phœbus turns an attacking serpent to stone.
scenes.stakes: The head risks being bitten by the serpent.

scenes.title: Reunion in the underworld
scenes.summary: Orpheus's ghost descends and finds Eurydice in the fields of the blessed, and they walk together; he can now safely look back at her.

scenes.title: The women become trees
scenes.summary: Lyæus roots the Edonian women to the ground, and they turn into oak trees as they struggle to flee.
scenes.stakes: The women are punished for murder by being rooted and transformed into trees.

alias_notes.explanation: Phœbus is a title of Apollo, whom the text elsewhere names as Orpheus's patron.
Lyæus, the 'loosener', is a name for Bacchus, god of the rites.
Edonian and Ciconian are Thracian peoples; the same women are meant.

notable_quotes.reason: Even a thrown stone is overcome by his music and falls like a suppliant.
The severed head's lyre still mourns as it floats down the river.

analysis.text: The power of art is shown and then defeated by mob frenzy and noise; yet Orpheus's music survives death, and love is restored in the underworld.
Transformation as punishment: the killers become rooted trees, and the serpent stone, answering violence with fixity.

legacy.text: The death and dismemberment of Orpheus became a recurrent subject in art, from ancient vase paintings to Renaissance and Symbolist painting.

fun_facts.text: The Hebrus is today's Maritsa (Evros) river, and Lesbos lies across the Aegean from its mouth.

language_notes.text: "Orgies" here means the wild nocturnal rites of Bacchus (Dionysus), not the modern sense; the women are Bacchantes in ecstatic worship.
Ciconians were a Thracian people; "matrons" means married women, here frenzied followers of Bacchus.
"Contemner" means one who scorns; the women accuse Orpheus of despising them.
The Berecynthian pipe was a shrill pipe tied to the worship of Cybele, from Mount Berecynthus in Phrygia, often used in frenzied ritual.
The thyrsus was a Bacchic staff tipped with a pine cone and wreathed in leaves or ivy; it was a ritual object, not a weapon.
The stag doomed in the morning sand alludes to Roman arena spectacles, where animals were hunted or thrown to dogs.
"Mænades" (Maenads) are the female followers of Bacchus, another name for the Bacchanals.
"Harrows" are toothed frames dragged over ploughed ground to break up soil.
The Hebrus is the main river of Thrace. Orpheus's head and lyre were thrown into it after the Thracian women killed him.
Methymna was a city on Lesbos. Lesbos was later famed for lyric poetry and music, which fits the arrival of Orpheus's head and lyre.
Phœbus is Apollo, god of music and poetry. He protects the head of Orpheus, a poet closely linked to him.
Orpheus had gone to the underworld once before to win back Eurydice. He lost her by looking back, so he recognizes the places.
Lyæus ('the loosener') is a title of Bacchus, god of wine. Orpheus was his bard, yet the Edonian women, Bacchantes, killed him.
Edonian means Thracian. The Edoni were a Thracian people, so 'Edonian matrons' are the Thracian women who killed Orpheus.

context_notes.text: Orpheus had shunned women after losing Eurydice, which is the "indifference" for which the Thracian women punish him.
Orpheus is called Apollo's bard because his musical gift was linked to Apollo, god of music; in tradition he was the son of Calliope, a Muse.
The fields of the blessed (Elysium) were the part of the underworld where the virtuous dead lived happily.
Here Orpheus can look back at Eurydice without harm. In the earlier story, looking back caused her to be lost again.

literary_notes.text: The stone is given human feeling, lying at his feet like a suppliant ashamed of its daring, showing the power of his music.
Comparing the women to birds mobbing an owl by day and to dogs on a stag shows Orpheus as helpless prey.
His voice, which charmed everything, now fails for the first time, as he speaks in vain to those who will not hear.
The narrator's cry to Jupiter expresses horror and pathos at the voice that moved rocks now fading into the air.
Addressing the dead Orpheus directly as "thee" heightens the lament and makes nature a chorus of mourners.
The banks 'reply' mournfully, as if the landscape itself joined in grief for Orpheus.
The look that destroyed Eurydice is now harmless, so the old fatal act becomes a happy repeated gesture.
The trapped bird compares the women's panic to a snared creature, showing their helpless struggle as they take root.
Speaking to 'you' draws the reader into the scene and confirms the half-human, half-tree image.
